title: The Great Compromise
description: A swing-state delegate at the 1787 Constitutional Convention must navigate the deadlock over representation between large and small states

metadata.title: The Great Compromise
metadata.description: A swing-state delegate at the 1787 Constitutional Convention must navigate the deadlock over representation between large and small states
metadata.author: Civics Education Team

reflection_questions: How did you balance the competing demands of large states for proportional representation and small states for equal representation? Which principle did you weigh most heavily and why?
The Connecticut Compromise succeeded historically by giving each faction a partial victory. When is a compromise that leaves everyone somewhat dissatisfied preferable to a clear victory for one side?
Consider the tension between national unity and state sovereignty that ran through these debates. How did your choices reflect your assumptions about where legitimate authority should reside?
What role did your personal credibility as a broker play in your ability to influence the outcome? How do real negotiators build and spend trust across factions?
The delegates chose to build durable institutions rather than win a momentary argument. How might a decision that satisfies one faction completely create instability that outlasts the victory?
reflection_prompts: Think about how your decisions reflected different theories of representation and federalism
Consider the real-world consequences on both small-state and large-state citizens for generations
Reflect on how the threat of a Convention collapse shaped what was possible
Consider how trust built with one faction constrained or enabled your later moves

1.title: The Deadlock
1.description: The State House in Philadelphia, mid-summer 1787. The air is thick and the mood tense.
1.narration:
The windows are shut against eavesdroppers, and the July heat is stifling. For weeks the Convention has circled the same wound: how shall the people be represented in the new Congress?

James Madison of Virginia leans forward, his voice precise. 'Representation must follow population. It is the only just measure. A government of the people cannot count Delaware's few thousand as equal to Virginia's throng.'

Across the room, William Paterson of New Jersey rises, jaw set. 'The small states did not enter this union to be swallowed. Equal suffrage in the legislature, or we go home—and the union dissolves with us.'

You represent a state that could tip either way. Every eye seems to drift toward delegates like you. The Convention teeters. How will you position yourself as the debate opens?

choices.text: Speak forcefully for the Virginia Plan—proportional representation is the only principled foundation
Endorse the New Jersey Plan—equal state representation protects the union's smaller members
Hold back and signal openness to a middle path, urging both sides to keep talking
Float a wholly new idea—perhaps representation weighted by population but checked by supermajority rules

2a.title: The Large States Rally
2a.description: Madison and the Pennsylvania delegation nod their approval.
2a.narration:
Your words land firmly on the side of the large states. Madison inclines his head; James Wilson of Pennsylvania thumps the table in agreement. 'At last, a delegate who reasons from first principles,' Wilson says.

But the small-state benches grow cold. Paterson and the Delaware delegates whisper among themselves, and Gunning Bedford of Delaware casts you a hard look. 'You have chosen your side,' he mutters. 'Remember that a plan the small states will not sign is no plan at all.'

The hall's temperature—political and literal—rises. You have gained powerful allies but hardened the fault line.

2b.title: The Small States Rally
2b.description: Paterson and the Delaware and Connecticut delegates lean toward you with relief.
2b.narration:
Your defense of equal representation draws grateful nods from the small-state benches. Paterson gives a curt, approving bow. 'A delegate who understands that sovereignty was not surrendered lightly,' he says.

But Madison's expression tightens. Wilson of Pennsylvania rises at once. 'Then you would have a handful of citizens in the small states outvote the multitudes in the large. That is not a republic—it is a distortion.' The Massachusetts delegation shakes their heads.

You have earned the trust of the smaller states, but the large states now regard you warily. The chamber feels perilously close to fracture.

2c.title: The Cautious Broker
2c.description: Both factions study you, uncertain but not hostile.
2c.narration:
You decline to plant your flag on either extreme, instead pressing both sides to keep the Convention alive. 'We did not come all this way to adjourn in failure,' you say. 'Surely there is ground between these poles.'

Roger Sherman of Connecticut catches your eye and gives a slow, thoughtful nod. Madison looks mildly impatient but does not object. Paterson seems reassured that you have not simply joined the large states.

You have spent no capital on either faction—but you have kept your standing as a potential honest broker, and you have bought the Convention time. Sherman drifts toward your seat during the recess.

2d.title: A Novel Proposal
2d.description: The delegates murmur as you sketch an unfamiliar framework.
2d.narration:
You propose something the Convention has not fully considered: a single chamber where seats are apportioned by population, but where any measure touching state interests requires a supermajority—giving small states a shield without equal seats.

The room stirs. It is clever, and several delegates lean in. But Sherman of Connecticut frowns. 'An ingenious contrivance,' he allows, 'yet supermajorities can paralyze as easily as they protect. Who decides which measures touch state interests?'

Madison is intrigued but skeptical; Paterson suspects a trick to deny equal representation outright. You have marked yourself as a thinker—but a untested framework carries risk when the union hangs by a thread.

3a.title: The Walkout Threat
3a.description: A recess. Bedford of Delaware confronts you in the corridor.
3a.narration:
During the recess, Gunning Bedford corners you, and his words are grave. 'The small states have discussed leaving. Some would sooner seek foreign alliances than submit to being governed by the large states' numbers alone.'

It is a shocking threat—and not entirely a bluff. If the small states walk, the whole enterprise collapses, and you helped push them toward the door. Roger Sherman appears beside you, calmer. 'There is a design,' Sherman says quietly, 'that might yet hold both wings of this house together. Would you hear it?'

How do you respond to the crisis you helped create?

choices.text: Hold firm—call Bedford's threat a bluff and insist the large states will not yield on principle
Listen to Sherman's design and lend your voice to a bicameral compromise
Privately reassure Bedford that you will help find protections for small states, even while backing proportional ideals

3b.title: The Large States Push Back
3b.description: A recess. Wilson and Madison seek you out.
3b.narration:
James Wilson finds you during the break, Madison at his side. 'You have given the small states false hope,' Wilson says. 'Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Massachusetts together hold the bulk of this nation's people and wealth. We will not ratify a charter that renders our citizens second-class.'

Madison adds, more measured: 'Yet we do not wish the union to shatter. If there is a structure that honors population without erasing the states entirely, I would consider it.'

Roger Sherman lingers nearby, ready to speak. You sense a hinge point. How do you proceed?

choices.text: Dig in for the small states—equal representation must be preserved even if the large states balk
Back Sherman's bicameral compromise as the way to honor both principles
Quietly assure Madison you will help secure proportional representation in at least one chamber

3c.title: Sherman's Design
3c.description: During the recess, Roger Sherman lays out his idea in low tones.
3c.narration:
Sherman of Connecticut speaks plainly, as is his habit. 'Let the first branch—the House—be apportioned by population, as the large states demand. Let the second branch—the Senate—give each state an equal voice, as the small states require. Neither wins wholly; neither loses wholly. The house stands on two legs.'

It is elegant. Because you spent no capital taking sides, both factions might accept your endorsement as fair-minded rather than partisan. 'I need delegates of standing to carry this,' Sherman says. 'Delegates whom neither camp distrusts. You are such a one.'

Will you champion the compromise?

choices.text: Champion the Connecticut Compromise wholeheartedly, using your neutral standing to sway both sides
Support the compromise but hedge, waiting to see which faction gains momentum first
Counter with your own untested framework instead, gambling on a cleverer solution

3d.title: The Proposal Falters
3d.description: Your novel framework is debated—and picked apart.
3d.narration:
For a day your supermajority scheme dominates the floor. But the questions Sherman raised prove fatal: no one can agree which matters would trigger the special threshold, and both factions fear the ambiguity could be exploited. The small states still want a guaranteed equal voice; the large states still resent any brake on their numbers.

Sherman rises at last. 'The delegate's ingenuity is real,' he says, 'but this house needs a plainer bargain that each side can grasp and trust. I offer one: a House by population, a Senate of equal states.'

Your credibility as a thinker survives, but your framework is set aside. The question now is whether you rally to Sherman's plainer design or press your own further.

choices.text: Gracefully concede and throw your weight behind Sherman's bicameral compromise
Insist on refining your framework, convinced it can still satisfy both sides

4a.title: The Union Fractures
4a.description: The small-state delegates gather their papers.
4a.narration:
You call Bedford's bluff—and it is not one. Over the following days, the Delaware and New Jersey delegations grow openly rebellious. Sherman's compromise, without a respected broker to carry it across the aisle, cannot gain the trust needed to hold.

The Convention grinds toward paralysis. You backed principle over accommodation, and the fragile threads binding large and small states begin to snap. The delegates weigh whether to press on or adjourn in failure.

4b.title: Quiet Reassurance
4b.description: You work the corridors, softening the small states' fears.
4b.narration:
You privately promise Bedford and his allies that you will fight for real protections, even as you speak for proportional ideals on the floor. It is a delicate double game, and it earns you a measure of the small states' trust back.

But whispered assurances are not a structure. Sherman watches you and remarks, 'Good will is not a constitution, friend. The house needs a design, not a promise.' Whether the union holds now depends on whether that good will can be forged into something durable before patience runs out.

4c.title: The Large States Recoil
4c.description: Wilson slams his hand on the table as you hold your ground.
4c.narration:
You refuse to yield an inch for the small states, and the large-state delegations react with fury. 'Then there is nothing to discuss,' Wilson snaps. Madison, gravely disappointed, notes that Virginia and Pennsylvania will never ratify a charter that ignores their populations.

The large states begin murmuring about forming their own compact. Without their consent, no union is possible. Sherman's plainer bargain languishes, unchampioned across the divide. The Convention lurches toward collapse as the delegates consider their final options.

4d.title: A One-Sided Tilt
4d.description: Your maneuvering favors one faction, unsettling the balance.
4d.narration:
You throw your weight toward securing proportional representation, working Madison's side of the room. The large states are pleased, but the small states sense they are being outmaneuvered rather than accommodated.

Sherman shakes his head. 'You have tilted the scales instead of balancing them. A compromise that one side merely tolerates is a truce, not a peace.' Whether such a lopsided arrangement can survive ratification—or whether it sows lasting resentment—remains to be seen as the Convention nears its verdict.

4e.title: The Hesitant Ally
4e.description: You endorse the compromise, but only halfway.
4e.narration:
You tell Sherman you favor his design—but you wait, watching to see which faction gains the upper hand before committing fully. Your caution costs you. Delegates who might have followed a bold, neutral broker instead see hesitation.

'The moment for a decisive voice was now,' Sherman says with quiet regret. The compromise still has life, carried by others, but your influence over it has dimmed. The Convention moves toward its reckoning with the outcome still uncertain.

4f.title: Stubborn to the End
4f.description: You cling to your framework as patience drains from the room.
4f.narration:
You insist your supermajority scheme can still work, and days pass in fruitless refinement. The delegates grow weary and irritable. The plainer compromise sits waiting, but your persistence has consumed precious time and goodwill.

'Ingenuity untethered from consensus is a kind of vanity,' one delegate remarks. Sherman's bargain may yet be adopted by others, but you have spent your standing chasing a solution the house would not embrace. The Convention approaches its final judgment.

4compromise.title: Carrying the Compromise
4compromise.description: You take Sherman's design onto the floor with conviction.
4compromise.narration:
You rise and speak for the bicameral bargain: a House apportioned by population, a Senate of equal states. Because you have not made yourself a partisan of either extreme, delegates on both benches listen without reflex hostility.

'The large states gain their principle in the first branch,' you argue. 'The small states gain their security in the second. Neither is asked to surrender what they cannot. This is not a defeat for anyone—it is the frame on which a lasting union can be built.'

Madison studies the design; Paterson and Bedford confer. The mood in the sweltering hall begins, at last, to shift. The Convention prepares to weigh the accumulated record of these deliberations and render its verdict.

resolution.title: The Convention Weighs Its Choice
resolution.description: The delegates assemble for the decisive reckoning. The heat, the exhaustion, the accumulated trust and mistrust—all of it converges.
resolution.narration:
The Convention gathers for the vote that will determine whether a nation is born or the effort dissolves. Every position you took, every corridor conversation, every faction you reassured or alienated now bears its weight.

Roger Sherman looks around the chamber. 'We have labored long,' he says. 'The question is whether this house has built enough trust across its divides to stand as one.'

The tally will turn not on any single speech but on the whole arc of the bargain you helped shape—or failed to. The delegates fall silent as the count begins.

5.grand_compromise.title: The Great Compromise
5.grand_compromise.description: The bicameral bargain is adopted to broad, if weary, satisfaction.
5.grand_compromise.narration:
By your steady, even-handed work, you earned the trust of both the large and small states and kept the union whole. The Convention adopts the Connecticut Compromise: a House of Representatives apportioned by population and a Senate in which every state, large or small, holds equal voice.

Because you never made yourself the creature of one faction, both sides accepted your advocacy as fair, and the bargain carried with genuine consent rather than grudging surrender. Madison, though he had wanted more, acknowledges the structure will endure. Sherman clasps your hand. 'This,' he says, 'is how a house is built to last—two legs, each bearing its share.'

The framework you helped forge will shape the representation of citizens for centuries to come.
5.grand_compromise.outcome_message: You brokered the Great Compromise with the full trust of both factions, securing a durable union.

5.durable_union.title: A Union Preserved
5.durable_union.description: The compromise passes, carried by cautious goodwill on both sides.
5.durable_union.narration:
The bicameral bargain is adopted. You did not command the total confidence of either faction, but you kept enough trust on both sides and preserved the Convention's stability through its darkest hours. The House will be proportional; the Senate will be equal.

The agreement is real, if less triumphant than it might have been—some delegates sign with reservations, and the memory of the deadlock lingers. Yet the union holds, and the essential frame endures. Sherman nods to you. 'Not every peace is a celebration,' he says. 'But this one will keep the house standing.'

The structure you supported becomes the foundation of American representation.
5.durable_union.outcome_message: The compromise passed and the union was preserved, though not every delegate was fully won over.

5.large_state_charter.title: The Large States Prevail
5.large_state_charter.description: A framework tilted toward population is adopted—over small-state objections.
5.large_state_charter.narration:
You threw your weight decisively behind the large states, and a charter favoring proportional representation is pushed through. Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Massachusetts are triumphant; their populations will dominate the new Congress.

But the small states sign under protest, if they sign at all. Bedford of Delaware warns that a union built on their resentment carries a hidden fracture. 'You have won the vote,' he tells you, 'but not our hearts. Remember which was harder to keep.' The structure favors the many at the expense of the small states' sense of security, and whispers of future discord follow the Convention out the door.

Representation now leans heavily toward the populous states, for better and for worse.
5.large_state_charter.outcome_message: You secured a proportional framework favoring large states, but at the cost of small-state trust and lasting resentment.

5.small_state_bloc.title: The Small States Hold the Line
5.small_state_bloc.description: Equal representation is preserved—over large-state fury.
5.small_state_bloc.narration:
You stood firmly with the small states, and a framework preserving equal state representation is adopted. Delaware, New Jersey, and Connecticut are grateful; their sovereignty is protected.

But the large states are embittered. Wilson of Pennsylvania declares that a government in which a minority of citizens can outvote the majority defies the very idea of a republic. Madison signs reluctantly, convinced the arrangement is unjust to the millions in the populous states. 'You have guarded the small,' he tells you, 'but wounded the principle of the whole.' The union survives, but the tension between numbers and equality remains raw and unresolved.

The small states' voice is secured, though the larger populations feel slighted.
5.small_state_bloc.outcome_message: You preserved equal representation for small states, but alienated the large states and left the majority feeling wronged.

5.fragile_truce.title: An Uneasy Truce
5.fragile_truce.description: A patched-together arrangement passes, satisfying no one fully.
5.fragile_truce.narration:
Through hesitation, hedging, or one-sided maneuvering, you failed to build the broad trust a lasting bargain requires. An arrangement is cobbled together, but it rests on goodwill too thin and structure too improvised to inspire confidence.

The delegates sign, but many do so uncertainly, and the memory of your wavering lingers. Sherman offers a rueful assessment: 'The house stands, but its foundations were laid in doubt. Such structures require constant repair.' The union endures for now, yet the unresolved strains suggest trouble ahead.

Representation is settled in name, but the deeper questions were never fully answered.
5.fragile_truce.outcome_message: A fragile truce held the union together, but weak trust and improvised structure left the settlement unstable.

5.collapse.title: The Convention Dissolves
5.collapse.description: The delegates gather their papers and depart in failure.
5.collapse.narration:
The trust between factions eroded past recovery. With the union's stability shattered, delegates on both sides conclude that no charter can be salvaged. One by one, the delegations withdraw.

The small states speak of seeking foreign protection; the large states murmur of forming their own compact. The great experiment at Philadelphia ends not with a signature but with an adjournment into uncertainty. Sherman, gathering his notes, says quietly, 'We came to build a house and could not agree on its frame. History will judge what we failed to do here.'

The deadlock over representation proved fatal, and the promise of a unified nation slips away—a sobering lesson in how a refusal to accommodate can undo even the most necessary endeavor.
5.collapse.outcome_message: The Convention collapsed as trust between factions failed, and the union dissolved into uncertainty.
